lead: Today’s two readings are both about a calling that seems to have failed. The Servant cries, “I have labored in vain”, and God answers by making his mission wider. At the supper Jesus is troubled, Judas goes out into the night, and Peter promises more than he can give. Yet at that very moment Jesus says, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified”. Psalm 71 prays from the womb onward, as the Servant does: “Upon you I have leaned from my birth”.

set: This is the second Servant Song. In the first, God spoke about the Servant. Now the Servant speaks for himself, and he addresses the coastlands and peoples far away. In Babylon the exiles felt forgotten (49:14). The song answers that weariness from within: even God’s chosen one has felt he has achieved nothing.
str: vv. 1–3: the call from the womb; mouth like a sword; “You are my servant”.
v. 4: the Servant’s discouragement and his trust.
vv. 5–6: God’s answer: the mission grows to the end of the earth.
kw: A polished arrow is kept hidden in the quiver until the moment it is needed. Long hiddenness is part of the Servant’s preparation, as it was in the thirty years at Nazareth.

In v. 4 the Servant says he has spent his strength for tōhû, the word used for the formless earth in Genesis 1:2. The word beside it, hebel, is the “vanity” of Ecclesiastes. He holds nothing back from God about how it feels.
See also 42:6. The Latin form of this phrase gives the Second Vatican Council’s Constitution on the Church its opening words, Lumen gentium, and the Council says at once that the light is Christ.
vv: The Lord called me before I was born, while I was in my mother’s womb he named me.
St Paul describes his own call in these words (Galatians 1:15; compare Jeremiah 1:5). A vocation begins earlier than any human decision.
“You are my servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified.”

“Israel” stands in nearly all manuscripts, yet in vv. 5–6 this servant has a mission to Israel. Here is the song’s riddle: the Servant both embodies the people and serves them. Christians see it resolved in Jesus, the faithful Israelite who gathers Israel and the nations. The people of Israel remain God’s own, whose gifts and calling are not withdrawn (Romans 11:29).
I will give you as a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.
God answers a complaint of failure not by making the work smaller but by making it larger.
ch: Old Simeon, holding the child, calls him “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (Luke 2:32). Paul and Barnabas take 49:6 as their own charter in Antioch of Pisidia (Acts 13:47). So the song belongs first to Christ, and then to those who share his mission. The Catechism lists it among the Songs that proclaim the meaning of the Passion (CCC 713). Those who feel their work has come to nothing can pray v. 4 honestly, including its second half: “yet surely my cause is with the Lord”.

set: We are at the supper, after the washing of the feet (13:1–20). John’s reader already knows the devil’s work in Judas (13:2). The Mass reading passes over vv. 34–35, the new commandment. The verses left in show three disciples around Jesus: the one who betrays, the one who rests close to him, and the one who boasts and will fall.
str: vv. 21–26: “One of you will betray me”; the disciple Jesus loved asks who; the piece of bread.
vv. 27–30: Satan enters; Judas goes out; night.
vv. 31–33: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified”; “Little children”.
vv. 36–38: Peter’s promise and the warning about the cock.
kw: The same verb is used at the tomb of Lazarus (11:33) and when his hour comes near (12:27). The Jesus who goes so firmly to death in John is not untouched by what is coming. Betrayal by a friend hurts him.
A morsel dipped in the shared dish. Many commentators think that to be offered it by the host was a mark of friendship. If so, the last thing Jesus does for Judas is to hold out his hand to him.
In John the glory of Jesus is not reached after the cross as though it were a mere reward. The cross is itself the place where God’s love is shown in full, and so where he is glorified.
vv: the one whom Jesus loved…was reclining next to him;

Greek has “on the bosom of Jesus”, the word used of the Son who is “close to the Father’s heart” (1:18). As the Son rests in the Father, so this disciple rests in the Son. The Gospel does not name him; ancient tradition sees him as John the son of Zebedee, while some modern scholars keep the question open.
So, after receiving the piece of bread, he immediately went out. And it was night.

A time of day and a state of soul. Jesus has said that whoever walks at night stumbles (11:10). St Augustine remarks that Judas was not harmed by something evil in the bread: he took a good thing badly (in substance).
“Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.”

Peter uses the very words of the Good Shepherd (10:11). He means them sincerely, but he has the order reversed: Jesus lays down his life for Peter first. After the Resurrection Peter will be called three times to love and will truly follow (21:15–19).
ch: The Church reads the two failures of this night together. Judas and Peter both fail their Lord. The difference shows itself after the fall, in Peter’s return. No one should say of any person that he is beyond mercy. The words “It was night” are followed at once by “Now the Son of Man has been glorified”: the darkest deed of the week is taken up into the plan of love.

qa: If Jesus foretold the betrayal, did Judas have any choice?

Yes. To know beforehand is not to force. The Catechism says that God sees all moments of time in his eternal present, so his plan includes each person’s response, and he permits the acts that flow from human blindness in order to bring about his plan of salvation (CCC 600). Judas acted, and answered for it.
study: Where have I felt, like the Servant, that I “labored in vain”? Can I also say the second half of his verse?
Where am I closest to Peter this week, promising much out of love but relying on my own strength?
